title: Nuclear-recoil quenching at 250 keV: Lindhard theory, the NEST power law and the energy-scale systematic of the LZ event
question: What does Lindhard theory predict for the xenon quenching factor L(E) at 50-300 keV, how do the NEST power law (Table S5) and LZ's contour scale compare, what energy-scale uncertainty at 250 keV follows from plausible slope/k variations and does it explain the +-23 keV systematic, and is the p(E) charge-yield break physics or artefact?
headline_result: Lindhard L rises as E^0.16 (beta_eff 1.15-1.19 vs NEST 1.10); anchored to the D-D calibration at 74.7 keV any Lindhard curve predicts 7-9% more quanta at 248 keV than Table S5 (P009's contour offset) and 244-249 keV for the event, reproducing LZ's 248 keV; the +-23 keV systematic equals a yield-slope uncertainty delta beta = 0.085 that AmBe cannot constrain because the break parameters absorb light-yield rescaling; the break reproduces Thomas-Imel recombination saturation (Ne(248) = 301.0 vs LZ 300.8)
model_or_mechanism: Lindhard quenching (Lewin-Smith g(eps)), analytic NEST v2 NR yields with LZ p(E) break, Thomas-Imel box recombination, D-D-anchored slope variations, light-yield-scale vs (a,b) degeneracy
builds_on: LZ arXiv:2609.02823 (Table S5, detector-response supplement); P009, P024, P043, P038
agent_tools: Read x16, Bash x11, Write x5, Edit x8
software_and_packages: python 3.12.13; numpy 2.5.3; scipy 1.18.1 (brentq, least_squares); pandas 3.0.5; matplotlib 3.11.2; nestpy 2.1.1 (validation via lzcommon.nest_nr_yields); common/lzcommon.py
